issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'full sensory reliving' suggests highly vivid, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which sits in marked tension with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' Those two can sometimes coexist, but as a three-item profile with shame on recall they pull in opposing directions and are clinically questionable together.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'Avoid enclosed spaces' is not clearly coherent with the rest of the profile for sexual assault as described here. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, delays, shame, and vivid reliving; enclosed spaces introduces a more specific situational avoidance that is not supported by the memory/threat content and looks disconnected from the formulation, especially since Triggers is not active in this case.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'When I remember the event I feel intense shame' and 'Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time.' Severe shame and terror on recall usually make disclosure difficult rather than easy, so this combination is clinically questionable within the same node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Ruminate about how to get even with assailant' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile for this trauma type and patient presentation. The Memory and Threat items emphasize shame, terror, hypervigilance, and avoidance, which is more consistent with fear-based post-assault PTSD; revenge-focused rumination pulls toward a different emotional/cognitive stance and lacks support elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the rest of the presentation. The dominant active formulation is Memory↔Threat↔Maladaptive Strategies around trauma recollection and danger monitoring after sexual assault; gambling for excitement/distracting oneself is too nonspecific and does not connect clearly to the patient's other selected threat and memory items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Enclosed Spaces' appears to be a trigger/avoidance cue rather than a maladaptive strategy, and it is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, shame, terror, and speechless recall; avoidance of enclosed spaces is a different contextual pattern that is not otherwise supported here.

vignette:
Marcus is a 53-year-old married social worker who presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after being sexually assaulted by an acquaintance in a parking garage adjacent to a community services building where he had worked for nearly two decades. The assault occurred late on a weeknight when Marcus had stayed after hours to complete case documentation. The garage was poorly lit, the elevator had been out of service, and he had taken the stairwell - a narrow, concrete enclosure that smelled of damp and exhaust - when the man, someone he recognised from a client support group, cornered him between two floors. The confinement of that stairwell, the footsteps that had closed in behind him before he understood what was happening, and the complete absence of any route of escape left an imprint that now organises much of Marcus's daily life.

In the months that followed, Marcus found that remembering the assault did not feel like recollection - it felt like return. When the memory surfaced, the terror he had experienced in that stairwell returned with it at the same pitch and urgency, as though his nervous system had never been informed that the event had ended. Alongside the terror came something he described as harder to carry: an intense, wordless shame. He knows what happened. He can place it in time and sequence. But when he tries to speak about it - to his wife, briefly to his primary care physician - the language simply is not there. He stops mid-sentence, gestures vaguely, and changes the subject. The memory, in this way, remains sealed and unprocessed, and it is precisely this quality - its rawness, its resistance to narrative - that has made the memories themselves feel dangerous. Because remembering produces terror and shame he cannot metabolise, Marcus has worked hard to push the memories out of his mind the moment they appear, treating suppression as the most reasonable available option. He has also begun spending long evening hours turning over, in exhaustive and circular detail, what he might do to confront or expose the man who assaulted him - fantasies of retribution that feel, in the moment, like the only form of agency available to him. These strategies - suppression, rumination about revenge - emerged directly from the unbearable quality of the memories themselves, an attempt to manage what he could not yet articulate.

The memories have also reshaped how Marcus reads the world around him. Having been attacked from behind in a confined space he believed was safe, he now experiences the environment as fundamentally unreadable and threatening. He scans constantly. At the office, in supermarkets, in corridors, he checks behind him with a regularity that has begun to draw quiet comment from colleagues. Unfamiliar settings - a new client's neighbourhood, a building he hasn't been to before - feel genuinely dangerous because he cannot pre-assess them, and he has begun declining field visits that would have been routine before. When a meeting runs long or a colleague is late to respond to a message, he does not register it as ordinary delay; he assumes something bad is unfolding. This pervasive sense of threat, in turn, drives him back toward the memories - scanning for details, trying to identify what he missed, what warning he should have read - which only re-exposes him to the terror and shame he is simultaneously trying to suppress. The loop is quiet but relentless. His threat monitoring, meanwhile, has reinforced every avoidance behaviour: he no longer uses the parking garage at work, refuses stairwells, and will not enter any enclosed or confined space if he can avoid it. These restrictions have accumulated into something his wife has noticed - a man who used to be physically easy in the world now mapping every room for exits before he can settle.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a supervision session in which he was unable to enter the small conference room where the meeting was scheduled, standing in the doorway until a colleague quietly suggested they move to a larger space. He said nothing that day, but he made the referral call the following morning. What he fears most is that something essential has been permanently altered in him. What he is hoping for, more cautiously, is to find words for what happened - to be able to say it plainly, once, without the terror coming with it.
